title: Word embeddings: word2vec and GloVe
text:
CHAPTER 17. LANGUAGE: EMBEDDINGS TO ATTENTION
SECTION 17.1. WORD EMBEDDINGS: WORD2VEC AND GLOVE

Computer vision was transformed by deep learning around 2012 (Chapter 16). Language followed, and the first step was a new way to represent words. Instead of treating each word as an arbitrary symbol, word embeddings represent each word as a dense vector of a few hundred real numbers, learned from large amounts of text, so that words with similar meanings have similar vectors. This section explains where the idea came from, how word2vec and GloVe learn such vectors, what the vectors capture, and their limits. Embeddings remain the first layer of every modern language model.

1. The problem with symbols

Classical natural language processing (NLP) represented a word as a "one-hot" vector: with a vocabulary of V words (often 100,000 or more), word number i is a vector of length V with a 1 in position i and zeros elsewhere. Any two different one-hot vectors are orthogonal: the dot product of "hotel" and "motel" is 0, exactly the same as "hotel" and "banana". Nothing about meaning is shared, so a model that learns something about "hotel" learns nothing about "motel". Statistical language models of the 1990s and 2000s, such as n-gram models that estimate P(word | previous n - 1 words) from counts, suffered from this: most long word sequences never appear in the training data, and smoothing methods could only partly compensate.

2. The distributional hypothesis

The key idea is old and comes from linguistics. Zellig Harris argued in the 1950s that words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings, and J. R. Firth's 1957 phrase "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" is the usual slogan. "Coffee" and "tea" appear near "cup," "drink," "hot" and "morning"; "coffee" and "carburetor" rarely share contexts.

Counting methods turned this into vectors. Build a co-occurrence matrix X, where X_ij is how often word j appears within a window (for example 5 words) of word i. Rows are long and sparse, so reduce them. Latent semantic analysis (LSA; Scott Deerwester, Susan Dumais and colleagues, 1990) applied a truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) to a term-document matrix:

    X approx U_k S_k V_k^T

keeping the top k singular values (a few hundred), and used the rows of U_k S_k as word vectors. Reweighting counts by pointwise mutual information (PMI) usually helps:

    PMI(i, j) = log [ P(i, j) / ( P(i) P(j) ) ]

PMI is positive when two words co-occur more than chance would predict. These count-based vectors already captured similarity, and they were used for information retrieval and essay grading.

3. Neural language models

Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent and Christian Jauvin ("A Neural Probabilistic Language Model," Journal of Machine Learning Research, 2003) proposed learning word vectors as part of a neural network that predicts the next word. Each of the previous n - 1 words is mapped through a shared lookup table C (a V x d matrix, one d-dimensional row per word), the vectors are concatenated, passed through a hidden tanh layer, and a softmax over the vocabulary gives P(next word). Training by backpropagation (Chapter 13) adjusts both the network and the embeddings. Because similar words get similar vectors, the model can generalize from "the cat is walking in the bedroom" to "a dog was running in a room". It outperformed strong n-gram baselines, but the softmax over a large vocabulary made training slow.

Ronan Collobert and Jason Weston (2008, and with colleagues in a 2011 JMLR paper, "Natural Language Processing (Almost) from Scratch") trained embeddings with a ranking objective (real text windows should score higher than windows with a random word substituted) and showed they help many tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition. Tomas Mikolov's recurrent neural network language models (around 2010) further improved language modeling and speech recognition.

4. word2vec

Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado and Jeffrey Dean at Google posted "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space" on arXiv in January 2013, followed by "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality" (Mikolov, Ilya Sutskever, Chen, Corrado, Dean; arXiv October 2013, NIPS 2013). The key decision was to drop the hidden layer and make the model as simple as possible, so it could be trained on billions of words on ordinary CPUs. They released the code as the word2vec tool, along with pretrained vectors, widely used ones being 300-dimensional vectors trained on Google News text (reported as about 100 billion words).

Two architectures:

  - Continuous bag of words (CBOW): predict the center word from the average of the vectors of its surrounding words.
  - Skip-gram: predict each surrounding word from the center word.

Skip-gram in detail. Each word w has two vectors: an input ("center") vector v_w and an output ("context") vector u_w, each of dimension d (typically 100 to 300). For a center word c and a context word o within the window, the full softmax model is

    P(o | c) = exp(u_o . v_c) / sum_(w in vocabulary) exp(u_w . v_c)

and training maximizes the sum of log P(o | c) over all (center, context) pairs in the corpus. The sum in the denominator runs over the whole vocabulary, which is too expensive. Two approximations were used: the hierarchical softmax (a binary tree over the vocabulary, costing about log2(V) operations) and, more popular, negative sampling.

Negative sampling (SGNS, skip-gram with negative sampling) replaces the multiclass prediction with binary classification: distinguish the real context word o from k "negative" words w_1..w_k drawn at random. For one pair the objective to maximize is

    log s(u_o . v_c) + sum_(i=1..k) log s(-u_(w_i) . v_c)

where s is the sigmoid. The negatives are drawn from the unigram distribution raised to the power 3/4, P(w) proportional to count(w)^(3/4), which samples rare words somewhat more often than their frequency. k is typically 5 to 20 for small datasets and 2 to 5 for large ones, as the paper recommended. Very frequent words like "the" were randomly discarded during training (subsampling), which both sped up training and improved vectors for rarer words.

A small worked number: if u_o . v_c = 2, then s(2) is about 0.88, so the model gives 88 percent probability that this is a real pair. The gradient of log s(x) with respect to x is 1 - s(x), about 0.12, so the update pushes the two vectors closer together a little more; for a negative pair with dot product 2, the gradient of log s(-x) is -s(x), about -0.88, a strong push apart.

After training, v_w (sometimes averaged with u_w) is used as the embedding of w. Similarity is measured by cosine similarity:

    cos(a, b) = (a . b) / ( |a| |b| )

5. Analogies and linear structure

The most famous result was that simple vector arithmetic captures relations. In "Linguistic Regularities in Continuous Space Word Representations" (Mikolov, Wen-tau Yih and Geoffrey Zweig, NAACL 2013), and in the word2vec papers, analogy questions "a is to b as c is to ?" were answered by finding the word whose vector is closest (by cosine) to

    v(b) - v(a) + v(c)

excluding a, b and c themselves. The standard example is king - man + woman, whose nearest neighbor is queen. Other relations included capital cities (Paris - France + Italy gives Rome), verb tenses and comparatives. The January 2013 paper introduced a test set of semantic and syntactic analogy questions on which accuracy could be measured. The exclusion of the input words matters: without it, the nearest vector is often one of the inputs, and later analyses showed analogy performance is less clean than the famous examples suggest. Still, the linear regularity was striking: directions in the space roughly correspond to relationships such as gender or country-capital.

6. GloVe

Jeffrey Pennington, Richard Socher and Christopher Manning of Stanford published GloVe ("Global Vectors for Word Representation") at EMNLP 2014. They combined the global statistics of count-based methods with the efficiency of word2vec-style training. Their observation: ratios of co-occurrence probabilities carry meaning. For example, P(solid | ice) / P(solid | steam) is large, P(gas | ice) / P(gas | steam) is small, and for a word like "water," related to both, the ratio is near 1. To make vector differences encode such ratios, they asked for

    w_i . w~_j + b_i + b~_j approx log X_ij

(w are word vectors, w~ context vectors, b biases), and fit it by weighted least squares over all nonzero entries of the co-occurrence matrix:

    J = sum_(i,j: X_ij > 0) f(X_ij) ( w_i . w~_j + b_i + b~_j - log X_ij )^2

with weighting f(x) = (x / x_max)^alpha for x < x_max, and 1 otherwise, using x_max = 100 and alpha = 3/4. The weighting prevents rare, noisy co-occurrences from dominating while capping the influence of very common pairs. The final vectors are w + w~. GloVe released vectors trained on corpora such as Wikipedia plus Gigaword and Common Crawl, and they became as widely used as word2vec.

7. Prediction and counting are close relatives

Omer Levy and Yoav Goldberg ("Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization," NIPS 2014) showed that skip-gram with negative sampling, at its optimum, implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix:

    u_j . v_i = PMI(i, j) - log k

where k is the number of negative samples. (For k = 5, the shift is log 5, about 1.61.) So the "neural" and "count" approaches are closely related, and much of word2vec's practical advantage came from design choices such as subsampling, the 3/4 smoothing and window weighting, which can also be applied to count methods.

8. Extensions

  - fastText (Piotr Bojanowski, Edouard Grave, Armand Joulin and Tomas Mikolov, Facebook AI Research; arXiv July 2016) represents each word as the sum of vectors of its character n-grams (for example "where" includes "<wh", "whe", "her", "ere", "re>"), so it can build vectors for rare and unseen words and handles languages with rich morphology, such as Mongolian, Turkish or Finnish, much better.
  - Subword tokenization: byte-pair encoding (BPE) for neural translation (Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch, 2015) splits rare words into frequent pieces. Modern language models use subword tokens (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) rather than whole words, and their first layer is an embedding table of the same kind as word2vec's lookup table.
  - Sentence and document embeddings: averaging word vectors, doc2vec, and later transformer-based sentence encoders, now widely used for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (Chapter 19).

9. Limits

  - One vector per word: "bank" (river) and "bank" (money) share a single vector, a mixture of senses. Contextual embeddings, in which a word's vector depends on its sentence, solved this: ELMo (Matthew Peters and colleagues, 2018) used bidirectional LSTMs, and BERT used transformers (Section 18.2).
  - Bias: embeddings learn the statistics of their training text, including social stereotypes. Tolga Bolukbasi and colleagues' 2016 paper, "Man is to Computer Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker? Debiasing Word Embeddings," showed gender stereotypes in word2vec vectors trained on Google News and proposed ways to reduce them. Similar problems, and the difficulty of fully removing them, carried over to large language models.
  - Embeddings capture association, not grounded understanding: they know that words appear together, not what the words refer to in the world.

10. Why it mattered

Word embeddings made "pretraining" central to NLP: learn general representations from large unlabeled text once, then reuse them in many tasks. This idea scaled up from a lookup table (2013) to contextual models (2018) to large pretrained transformers (Chapters 18 and 19). They also popularized the geometric view of meaning, in which concepts are directions and regions in a high-dimensional vector space, which is still how researchers try to interpret what large models represent.

11. Summary

  - One-hot vectors share nothing between words; dense embeddings place similar words close together.
  - The distributional hypothesis (Harris, Firth, 1950s) underlies all embedding methods; LSA (1990) used SVD of counts.
  - Bengio and colleagues (2003) learned embeddings inside a neural language model.
  - word2vec (Mikolov and colleagues, 2013): skip-gram and CBOW, trained efficiently with negative sampling; analogies like king - man + woman approx queen.
  - GloVe (Pennington, Socher, Manning, 2014) fits word vectors to log co-occurrence counts by weighted least squares.
  - Skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix (Levy and Goldberg, 2014).
  - Limits: one vector per word sense, learned social biases; contextual embeddings and subword tokens followed.
